1/5 External contracts can seize execution control flow when called.

2/5 In reentrancy attacks, they call back before the initial invocation finishes.

3/5 These recursive callbacks let separate function invocations interact undesirably.

4/5 The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern updates state before making external calls.

Unchecked low-level calls can fail while execution continues, causing unexpected behavior. Review low-level call sites and check their return values to handle failures correctly.

2/5 Unprotected withdrawal bugs sometimes stem from unintentionally exposing initialization functions.

3/5 In legacy Solidity <0.4.22, misnaming a constructor places code in runtime bytecode for anyone to call.

4/5 Implement access controls so only authorized parties can initiate withdrawals per contract requirements.

Missing access controls allow malicious actors to withdraw Ether from contract accounts. Implement access controls so only authorized parties can initiate withdrawals, according to the contract's requirements.

1/5 Price oracle manipulation exploits vulnerabilities to alter contract execution logic.

2/5 This can lead to unauthorized actions, fund loss, and broader logic exploitation.

3/5 Contracts should aggregate multiple oracle and DEX sources while rejecting anomalous outliers.

4/5 Use Time-Weighted Average Prices (TWAPs) over sufficient windows and reject stale prices exceeding thresholds.

5/5 Implement fail-safe behaviors that halt sensitive operations when oracle data is suspicious or unavailable.

External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately, potentially causing a denial-of-service condition in the calling contract. To reduce this impact, isolate each external call into its own recipient-initiated transaction rather than batching them together.
